summary: This informational RFC specifies a way for a host to use the Port Control Protocol to indicate which connections should be protected against network failures. Those connections then get high-availability treatment on the network side, since applications and users often know best which flows matter.

eli5.summary: You can tell the network which of your conversations are the important ones, so it takes extra care to keep them from dropping.

subtitle: Let applications tell the network which connections matter for uninterrupted service.

tldr.problem: Networks struggle to identify which connections are business-critical without guessing. Applications and users know best which flows should survive network failures.
tldr.mechanism: PCP (Port Control Protocol) adds a CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED option that lets applications signal the network: 'protect this connection.' The network then replicates state between active and backup systems so failover is transparent.
tldr.outcome: Applications can protect critical connections like VoIP calls or important file transfers, while the network saves resources by not protecting every connection.

today: RFC 7767 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It documents a proposed PCP extension for high-availability applications.

sections.title: Introduction to Connection Protection
sections.content:
Check-pointing is the process of copying a connection's state from an active network device to a backup so that when the active fails, the backup takes over without the user noticing. RFC 7767 defines a way for applications to tell the network which connections should be check-pointed.

The problem with today's systems: the network has to guess which connections matter. It sees a long-lived connection and assumes it is critical. But that is wrong. A casual video stream might run for hours, while an urgent business call might last seconds. Users know which connections matter; the network should not have to guess.
sections.eli5: When a car repair shop has two phone lines and one breaks, the shop owner knows which calls are most important. The network should let the owner tell it which calls to protect, not make a guess.

sections.title: Why Heuristics Fail
sections.content:
Networks today use heuristics—rules of thumb—to pick connections to protect. They might check how long a connection has lived or what protocol it uses. But heuristics are not smart:

  • A flow can be critical for one user but not another. Gold-level subscribers may care about their video stream; free-tier users do not.
  • A connection may not be long-lived but still critical. A VoIP call lasts minutes, not hours, yet users demand uninterrupted service.
  • Heuristics are not deterministic. The same connection type may or may not be protected depending on other network conditions.

This wastes resources: protecting connections that do not matter, and failing to protect ones that do.
sections.eli5: If a teacher always picked the tallest student to be class president, sometimes they would pick a quiet kid who did not want the job. Better to ask the students who wants it.

sections.title: The CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED Option
sections.content:
RFC 7767 adds a CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED option (code 192) to PCP. It is simple: a 4-byte header with no data. The option has zero length and carries no parameters—it is just a flag that says 'this connection is critical.'

An application sends a PCP MAP or PEER request that includes CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED. The PCP server (a network device) receives it and checks: do we have resources to protect this? If yes, it tags the connection and replicates its state to the backup. If no, it processes the request normally but does not echo back the CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED option, which signals to the client that check-pointing was denied.
sections.eli5: It is like raising your hand in class. You send a message that says 'check-point me.' The teacher either checks you off on a list or says they are too busy.

sections.title: How It Works in Practice
sections.content:
When a PCP client wants to protect a connection, it sends CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED in the MAP or PEER request. The PCP server must check whether it has resources. Networks SHOULD limit how many connections each client can ask to protect—this prevents one misbehaving app from hogging backup capacity.

To update a mapping, the client sends a renewal request. To enable check-pointing, it includes CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED. To disable it, it omits the option. The server updates the check-point flag accordingly.

A key assumption: the network on which PCP messages travel is trusted. If an attacker can intercept PCP messages, they could strip the option from critical flows or add it to unimportant ones to exhaust resources. If the network is not trusted, PCP authentication (RFC 7652) should be enabled.

Importantly, what to check-point and how are implementation choices left to the network. Some devices might store full session state; others might store just enough to resume. This flexibility lets vendors optimize for their hardware.
sections.eli5: You tell the network 'check-point this call.' The network says yes or no. If you renew your call and do not ask for check-pointing anymore, the network stops protecting it. An honest network listens; a network under attack might cheat.

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases
sections.content:
A streaming app is installed on three homes: A, B, and C. For A, the app is critical service. For B, it is entertainment. For C, the user can choose which shows to protect.

When A streams, all flows get CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED. When B streams, none do. When C chooses a favorite show, only that flow gets the flag. The result: A loses nothing on failover; B saves resources; C picks what matters to them.

Another example: a streaming provider offers three tiers. Gold subscribers: all flows protected. Silver: some protected. Bronze: none protected. The provider uses login credentials to determine tier and configure the app automatically.

A third use case: VoIP apps should check-point all calls, but emergency calls get priority because they matter most. The app can identify emergency calls (e.g., by recognizing a dialed number) and signal them to the network.
sections.eli5: Different families stream different shows. Mom's favorite soap opera gets check-pointing; the kids' game does not. Everyone pays less because the network protects only what each family asked for.
